title: AI and prompting at work
desc: What AI chatbots are, how to prompt them, and how to use them safely in sales work

src.l: Microsoft Learn: What is Microsoft Copilot
Microsoft Learn: Copilot data, privacy and security

lessons.title: What an AI chatbot really is

pages.h: A chatbot built on a language model
pages.t: Tools like Claude, ChatGPT and Copilot are built on a large language model. It is trained on a huge amount of text to generate language. It can write, summarise, translate and analyse text.
g: Large language model: software trained on lots of text to understand and generate language.
A chat window where you type to an LLM and it answers.

pages.h: It predicts, it does not look up
pages.t: At its core, a language model learns to predict the next word. It is then tuned to follow instructions. So it is not a database of verified facts. It produces fluent text that fits your request.
g: A small chunk of text, often part of a word, that the model reads and writes.

pages.h: Good at language, weaker at facts
pages.t: It is strong at drafting, rewriting, summarising and brainstorming. It is weaker at exact facts and precise numbers, and at fresh news unless it can search the web. Treat it like a fast, eager junior colleague whose work you still check.

quiz.q: What is a large language model mainly trained to do?
o: Store a verified fact for every question
Process and generate language, starting from predicting the next word
Search the live internet for every answer
quiz.w: Language models are trained on lots of text to generate language, and basic training is next-word prediction.

quiz.q: Which task is a typical STRENGTH of a chatbot?
o: Giving an exact current stock level
Rewriting a rough email into a clear one
Guaranteeing a legal answer is correct
quiz.w: Drafting and rewriting are core language strengths. Exact and current facts are weaker spots.

quiz.q: A good mental picture for working with AI is:
o: An all-knowing expert you never need to check
A calculator that is always exact
A fast, eager junior colleague whose work you review
quiz.w: It is helpful and quick, but it can be wrong, so you review the result.

src.l: Microsoft Learn: Copilot data, privacy and security

pages.t: A hallucination is text that sounds fluent and sure but is false or unsupported. It can invent a product spec, a quote or a source. Even good tools do this sometimes, so check anything that matters before you use it.
g: When an AI states something false or made up as if it were true.

pages.t: You can lower the risk. Give it the source text to work from. Tell it to say I don't know when unsure. Ask it to quote the passage that backs each claim. These help a lot, but they do not remove the risk fully.

Anything you paste goes to a service run by someone else. Never paste customer data, prices, contracts or passwords into a public tool. Use only tools your company approves, and check the policy. Work accounts and personal accounts can have different terms.
g: A free or personal AI account, outside your company's agreements.

quiz.q: What is a hallucination?
o: A slow reply from the tool
Fluent text that is false or made up
A message the tool refuses to answer
quiz.w: Hallucinations sound convincing but are wrong or unsupported.

quiz.q: Which prompt habit helps reduce hallucinations?
o: Telling it to always sound certain
Allowing it to say it does not know and giving it source text
quiz.w: Permission to admit uncertainty plus real source text reduces invented facts.

quiz.q: A colleague wants to paste a customer's price list into a free chatbot. What do you say?
o: Fine, if the chat is deleted afterwards
Do not, unless the company has approved that tool and use
Fine, if you remove the logo
quiz.w: Confidential data should only go into company-approved tools. Check the policy first.

quiz.q: Do hallucination-reducing tricks remove the problem completely?
o: No, they reduce it, so important facts still need checking
quiz.w: Anthropic's own guidance says these techniques reduce, not eliminate, hallucinations.

lessons.title: A good prompt: task, context, format

pages.t: A prompt is what you type. Anthropic suggests imagining a brilliant but new employee who lacks context about your work. The clearer you explain the task, the better the result. Vague in, vague out.
g: The instruction or question you give the AI.

pages.t: Say why you need it and who it is for. Then say the shape you want: three bullets, a 100 word email, a table. Example: Summarise this thread for my manager in three bullets, plain language.
Anthropic's tip: show your prompt to a colleague with little background. If they would be confused, the AI will be too. OpenAI's guide agrees that explicit instructions help the model.

quiz.q: Which prompt is better?
o: Summarise these notes in three bullets for my manager, plain language, no jargon
quiz.w: It names the task, audience, format and style.

quiz.q: What does adding context do?
o: It helps the AI aim at your real goal
quiz.w: Knowing why and for whom helps the AI give a more targeted answer.

quiz.q: What is the colleague test?
o: Ask a colleague to write the prompt
Send the answer to a colleague
Would a person with little background understand the prompt?
quiz.w: If a newcomer would be confused, the AI probably will be too.

pages.t: Examples are one of the most reliable ways to steer tone and format. Paste a sample of what good looks like, such as one of your own emails, and say: write the new one in this style. A few examples improve consistency.
g: Giving the AI a few example inputs and outputs so it copies the pattern.

pages.t: One sentence can focus the answer: You are an experienced sales coach. A role shapes tone and viewpoint. It does not give the AI real experience, so it does not make facts more correct.

When you paste notes, mark them clearly: Here are my notes: ... Here is the email I received: ... Anthropic and OpenAI both advise structure, such as labelled sections, so the AI does not mix instructions with content.

quiz.q: You want emails that sound like you. What helps most?
o: Pasting one or two of your own emails as examples
quiz.w: Examples steer tone and structure reliably.

quiz.q: What does giving a role such as sales coach do?
o: Makes sure every fact is true
quiz.w: A role shapes how it answers, but it does not guarantee correctness.

quiz.q: Why label the parts of a long prompt?
o: So instructions and pasted content do not get mixed up
It is required by every tool
quiz.w: Clear structure helps the AI tell your instructions from your material.

lessons.title: Iterate and ask for questions back

pages.h: The first answer is a draft
pages.t: Prompting is a conversation. If the answer misses, do not start over. Say what to change: shorter, warmer, remove the second paragraph, add a clear next step. OpenAI also notes that output varies between runs.

For bigger tasks, end with: Before you start, ask me up to five questions you need answered. This stops the AI guessing about audience, goal and details. This can give a better first draft with less back and forth.

A useful pattern is draft, then review, then improve. Ask: Check this against my requirements and list anything missing or unsupported. It is a helper to catch slips, not a replacement for your own read.

quiz.q: The answer is close but too long. What next?
o: Start a new chat from scratch
Reply asking for it shorter and say what to cut
quiz.w: Iterating in the same chat is the normal way to refine.

quiz.q: Why tell the AI to ask you questions first?
o: It avoids guessing about missing details
quiz.w: Questions fill gaps in your brief before it writes.

quiz.q: Draft, review, improve is an example of:
quiz.w: Asking it to review its own draft against criteria can catch slips, but you still read it too.

src.l: Microsoft Learn: What is Microsoft Copilot

pages.t: Paste your rough text and ask for a clearer, shorter or friendlier version. Ask for three subject lines. Ask it to make a reply polite but firm. Always read the result and keep your own voice before sending.

AI can translate between languages you work in and turn messy call notes into a structure: summary, open questions, next steps. Have a native speaker check important customer translations, since tone and idioms can slip.

Use it for ideas: questions to ask a customer, objections to expect, ways to open a call. It is a thinking partner. Give it public information only, never confidential customer details unless your company's approved tool allows it.

quiz.q: You have messy call notes. A good use of AI is to:
o: Send the raw notes to the customer
Ask for a summary, open questions and next steps
quiz.w: Turning notes into structure is a strength of language models.

quiz.q: Before sending an AI-written email you should:
o: Send it straight away to save time
Read it, fix facts and tone, then send
quiz.w: You are responsible for what goes out under your name.

quiz.q: An important Finnish or Danish customer mail was translated by AI. Smart step?
o: Have a fluent speaker check key wording
Translate it back and forth twice
quiz.w: Tone and idiom errors are easy to miss, so check what matters.

quiz.q: Which input is safest to give a public chatbot when brainstorming?
o: Public product facts and a general customer type
quiz.w: Stick to public, non-confidential information in public tools.

lessons.title: Research, call prep and spotting errors

pages.h: Prep a call with public info
pages.t: Ask for a plan: I call a small IT reseller next week. List ten good opening questions and likely concerns. It speeds up thinking. For facts about a real company, use their own website and treat AI as a starting point.
Be careful with: exact numbers, dates, product names and model numbers, quotes and links, and anything that sounds too neat. Made-up sources can look real. A confident tone is not evidence of truth.

Ask which source backs each claim, then open that source yourself. Ask the same question twice or in another way and compare. For anything customer-facing, confirm with the vendor or an official page.

quiz.q: Which part of an AI answer deserves the closest check?
o: Exact numbers, product names and quoted sources
quiz.w: Specific facts and sources are where invented details hide.

quiz.q: The AI cites a web article. What do you do?
o: Ask the AI if it is sure
Open the link or source and confirm it says that
quiz.w: Check the source yourself. Citations can be invented.

quiz.q: Comparing answers from several runs helps because:
o: Inconsistencies can point to a made-up detail
quiz.w: Anthropic lists comparing multiple outputs as a way to spot hallucinations.

src.l: Claude Help: Chat search and memory

pages.t: A Claude project is a workspace with its own chats, uploaded files and written instructions. Claude uses that material in every chat inside the project. Good for one topic you return to, like a call-prep routine.
g: A workspace in Claude holding files, instructions and chats for one topic.

pages.t: When Claude makes something substantial, such as a document, slide deck, dashboard or small tool, it can open it beside the chat as an artifact. You can edit it, find it later in the Artifacts tab, export it, and share it when ready.
g: A standalone piece of work Claude creates, shown next to the chat.

pages.t: Claude can carry context across chats through memory, and can search past chats on paid plans. You can view, edit or delete what it saved, pause it, or use an incognito chat. On work plans, an owner decides if memory is on. Features differ by plan.
g: Facts Claude saves from chats to use in later ones.

quiz.q: What does a Claude project hold?
o: Chats, files and instructions for one topic
quiz.w: Projects bundle files, instructions and chat history.

quiz.q: What is an artifact?
o: A standalone piece of work like a document or slide deck beside the chat
quiz.w: Artifacts are substantial outputs you can edit, export and share.

quiz.q: You do not want a chat saved to memory. Which option exists?
quiz.w: Claude's memory help page describes pausing memory and incognito chats, which are not saved to memory.

quiz.q: Why say features differ by plan?
o: Availability and settings vary, so check your own account and company rules
quiz.w: Limits and who controls memory differ between plans, such as team and enterprise.

lessons.title: Microsoft Copilot in Outlook, Teams, Word, Excel

src.l: Microsoft Learn: What is Microsoft Copilot
Microsoft Learn: Copilot data, privacy and security

pages.t: Microsoft's overview lists in-app help: Outlook drafts emails, summarises threads and gives tone coaching. Teams summarises and transcribes meetings and captures action items. Word drafts, rewrites and summarises. Excel analyses data and suggests formulas.

pages.h: Licence and setup decide what you get
pages.t: Microsoft now calls it simply Microsoft Copilot, and says experiences vary by licence and tenant setup. Some versions only use the web and what you paste in. The fuller add-on version can use your work emails, files and meetings. Ask IT which version your company has.

Microsoft states Copilot only shows work data you already have permission to see, and that prompts, responses and work data are not used to train the underlying models. It still can be wrong, so Microsoft tells users to review output before sharing.

quiz.q: Which is listed as a Copilot function in Teams?
o: Summarising and transcribing meetings and capturing action items
quiz.w: Microsoft's overview names meeting summaries, transcripts and action items.

quiz.q: Why might your Copilot differ from a colleague's?
quiz.w: Experience depends on licence and tenant configuration.

quiz.q: What does Microsoft say about permissions?
o: It only surfaces data you already have access to
quiz.w: Copilot respects the user's existing permissions.

quiz.q: Copilot drafts a customer reply in Outlook. You should:
quiz.w: Microsoft says output is not guaranteed factual and should be reviewed.

pages.t: Instead of one giant request, chain small ones: 1 summarise the notes, 2 list the risks, 3 draft the follow-up email, 4 check it against the notes. You can inspect each step and fix problems early.

When a prompt works, keep it. Write a reusable version with blanks: Customer type: [..]. Goal: [..]. Tone: [..]. Store it in your notes or a Claude project. OpenAI also stresses testing and iterating prompts, since outputs vary.

A workflow follows steps someone fixed in advance. An agent chooses its own next steps and tools. Anthropic notes agents are more flexible but cost more, are slower and can compound errors. Start with the simplest thing that works.
g: An AI that decides its own steps and uses tools, such as search or files, to reach a goal.

quiz.q: Why split a big task into steps?
o: You can check each step and catch problems early
quiz.w: Chaining lets you review intermediate results.

quiz.q: What is a good reusable prompt template?
o: A prompt that says do your best
A saved prompt with blanks for customer type, goal and tone
quiz.w: Templates keep a working structure and fill in the variable parts.

quiz.q: Difference between a workflow and an agent?
o: Workflow follows fixed steps, agent picks its own steps
quiz.w: Anthropic defines workflows as predefined paths and agents as self-directing.

quiz.q: Anthropic's advice on complexity:
o: Use the simplest solution that works
Never use more than one prompt
quiz.w: Add complexity only when simpler options fall short.

lessons.title: When not to use AI: bias, limits and GDPR

pages.h: Skip AI when stakes and secrecy are high
pages.t: Do not use it as the final word on contracts, legal or financial advice, or exact specs. Do not feed it secrets or personal data without approval. And do not use it to judge people, like a colleague's performance or a candidate.

Models learn from human text, so output can reflect bias in that data and may be less reliable for some groups or topics. It has no real understanding of your customer. NIST's AI risk framework is a voluntary guide for managing such risks.
g: Output that unfairly favours or ignores some people or views, often learned from the training text.

pages.t: Personal data is anything about an identifiable person, like a name with an email. GDPR principles include data minimisation and purpose limitation. So share the least data needed, and ask your company before using AI on contact details. The EU AI Act also expects people to be told when they talk to a chatbot.
g: EU law on how organisations may handle personal data.
Use only the data you really need.

quiz.q: Which use is the riskiest?
o: Pasting a customer list with names and emails into an unapproved tool
Rewriting your own public blog post
quiz.w: Personal data in an unapproved tool raises privacy and GDPR problems.

quiz.q: Which is personal data under GDPR?
o: Any information about an identifiable living person
quiz.w: The Commission defines it as information about an identified or identifiable person.

quiz.q: What does data minimisation mean in practice?
o: Share only what is needed for the task
quiz.w: It is one of the seven GDPR principles.

quiz.q: Why can AI output be biased?
o: It learns from human-written text that can contain bias
quiz.w: Training data shapes output, including its flaws.
